title: Not even Zeus
hook: "I'll chain your leg." "My leg, yes; my will, not even Zeus can conquer" (Discourses 1.1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: grammar, gold, and Zeus explaining his one gift. Your line was the gift of use. Which impression did you look at before agreeing? Day three hundred ninety.

A tyrant leans across the table and lists what he can do to you. Chains. Prison. Worse. Epictetus stages this scene in the first discourse as a quick back-and-forth, almost like a comedy sketch. He wasn't writing from the safe side of power. He grew up enslaved, with no say over his own body, and that gives his answers a particular weight. Notice who gets the funny lines. It isn't the man with the chains. Today: not even Zeus.
screen: `A TYRANT LISTS WHAT HE CAN DO.` → `CHAINS. PRISON. WORSE.` → `NOT EVEN ZEUS.`

segments.voice: First, the rehearsal. Later in the first discourse, Epictetus runs through the hard things. I must die. Must I die groaning too? I must be chained. Must I also whine about it? I must be exiled. Does anyone stop me from going with a smile, cheerful and calm? Second, the scene. Tell me your secrets, says the tyrant. I won't. That's up to me. Then I'll chain you. What are you saying, man? Chain me? You'll chain my leg. My will, not even Zeus can overpower. I'll throw you in prison. You mean my little body. I'll cut off your head. Well, when did I ever tell you mine was the only neck in the world that couldn't be cut? Third, the word. The will he means is prohairesis, the power to choose, to judge, to assent or refuse. In the Discourses it names the part of you that's truly yours. A tyrant can move your body anywhere. He can't make you agree that his threat is your harm. Fourth, the life behind it. Later writers told a story that Epictetus' master once twisted his leg, and Epictetus calmly warned, you'll break it. When it broke, he said: didn't I tell you? Nobody knows if that happened, and another ancient source says he was simply lame from illness. But the Discourses never ask us to pretend chains don't hurt. They ask a narrower question: inside this constraint, what is still yours? These, Epictetus says, are the things to rehearse, to write down every day, to practice. Not because a tyrant is coming. Because small chains come every week.
screen: `MUST I DIE GROANING TOO?` · `MY LEG, YES. MY WILL, NOT EVEN ZEUS.` · `PROHAIRESIS: THE POWER TO CHOOSE.` · `INSIDE THE CONSTRAINT, WHAT'S YOURS?` · then, large: `NOT EVEN ZEUS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one constraint you're living inside right now. A job you can't leave yet. An illness. A tight budget. A family situation. A body that won't do what it used to. Name it plainly. Then ask Epictetus' question: inside this, what is still mine? How I speak. What I notice. What I agree to. Where I put my attention. Find one thing, and rest there. The bell holds the time.
Not even Zeus. Epictetus to the tyrant: you'll chain my leg, but my will, not even Zeus can overpower. Today's word.
Your line: not even zeus. Find freedom inside one constraint today: name what's fixed, then find one thing inside it that's still yours. Day three hundred ninety.

howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism often rehearse hard situations in advance and ask, inside each constraint, what still belongs to them: their choices, judgments and attention.

fork.setup: the tyrant says: I'll chain you. what does Epictetus answer?
options: you'll chain my leg. my will, not even Zeus can overpower.
fork.reveal: the body can be chained; the power to choose and judge can't be forced, not even by Zeus.

original.note: Greek: choice, will, the power to choose, Epictetus' word for the self that's truly ours.

trapdoor: what you thought: mind over matter.
what it means: the body can be chained, but no one can force your judgment or your choice.
what a scholar hears: prohairesis, Epictetus' central word, from a teacher who grew up enslaved and was later said to be lame.

sources.ref: Origen, Against Celsus 7.53 (the leg story); Simplicius, Commentary on the Enchiridion (lameness)

notes: Discourses 1.1 paraphrased: 'I must die: must I die lamenting? be fettered: lamenting too? exiled: does anyone hinder me from going with a smile?'; the tyrant dialogue: secrets, chains ('my leg you will fetter, but my will not even Zeus can overpower'), prison ('my body'), beheading ('when did I tell you that I alone had a neck that cannot be severed?'); these things philosophers should rehearse and write daily. Confirm sections; Long 1877 could be quoted if verified.
The broken-leg story is from Celsus as reported by Origen, Contra Celsum 7.53; Simplicius and the Suda attribute lameness to illness/rheumatism. Presented as uncertain. Confirm.
Greek προαίρεσις: confirm it is the word in 1.1 for 'will'.
